question: Which State body enforces health and safety law on Irish construction sites?
optionA: The Health and Safety Authority
optionB: SOLAS, which runs Safe Pass
optionC: The local county council
optionD: The Construction Industry Federation
explanation: The Health and Safety Authority (HSA) inspects workplaces and enforces the 2005 Act and its regulations. SOLAS runs the Safe Pass programme but does not enforce site safety law.

question: Which law sets out the general duties of employers and employees at work in Ireland?
optionA: The Building Control Act 2007
optionB: The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005
optionC: The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997
optionD: The Planning and Development Act 2000 and its rules
explanation: The 2005 Act is the main Irish health and safety statute. The Construction Regulations 2013 are made under it and add duties specific to building sites.

question: Which regulations set the specific health and safety duties for construction work in Ireland?
optionA: The Building Regulations 1997
optionB: The Fire Services Act 1981
optionC: The Construction Regulations 2013
optionD: The Planning and Development Regulations 2001
explanation: The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work (Construction) Regulations 2013 cover project supervisors, Safe Pass, site safety representatives, excavations and other construction duties.

question: Under the Construction Regulations 2013, which of these workers must hold a valid Safe Pass card?
optionA: A clerk in the site office
optionB: A client visiting on a site tour
optionC: An architect at a site meeting
optionD: A general construction operative
explanation: Schedule 4 applies to craft and general construction workers, on-site security workers and others the Minister prescribes. Office staff, supervised visitors and design professionals are not covered.

question: Apart from craft and general workers, which group named in the 2013 regulations needs Safe Pass?
optionA: On-site security staff
optionB: Canteen and catering staff
optionC: Visiting sales representatives
optionD: Show house visitors
explanation: Regulation 4(2) names persons undertaking on-site security work alongside craft and general construction workers. HSA guidance lists canteen and sales staff as not needing it.

question: Who on a site must coordinate arrangements so that workers hold valid Safe Pass cards?
optionA: The client
optionB: The PSCS
optionC: The architect
optionD: The local authority
explanation: Regulation 19 makes the project supervisor for the construction stage (PSCS) coordinate arrangements so that every worker who needs one holds a valid safety awareness card.

question: Besides the PSCS, who must make sure each worker under their direct control holds a valid Safe Pass card?
optionA: The worker's trade union
optionB: The owners of the next-door site
optionC: Their contractor or employer
optionD: The HSA's local inspector
explanation: Regulation 25 places the duty on every contractor or other person under whose direct control people work. The PSCS coordinates; the employer must check its own workers.

question: What does PSCS stand for on an Irish construction project?
optionA: Principal Site Contractor for Safety
optionB: Public Safety Compliance Service
optionC: Project Safety and Construction Supervisor
optionD: Project Supervisor Construction Stage
explanation: The PSCS is appointed by the client to manage and coordinate health and safety during the construction stage. The PSDP does the same at the design stage.

question: Which duty holder is responsible for health and safety during the design of a project?
optionA: The PSDP
optionB: The PSCS
optionC: The site safety representative
optionD: The safety officer
explanation: The project supervisor for the design process (PSDP) coordinates designers and prepares the preliminary safety and health plan before work starts on site.

question: Under section 13 of the 2005 Act, which of these is a duty of every employee?
optionA: Write the site's safety statement
optionB: Report defects that could endanger anyone
optionC: Appoint the contractor's own safety officer
optionD: Notify the whole project to the HSA
explanation: Section 13 requires employees to report defects in the workplace, equipment or system of work as soon as practicable. The safety statement and notification are duties of the employer and client.

question: What does the 2005 Act require of an employee about alcohol and drugs?
optionA: Only to avoid alcohol before the noon break
optionB: To declare any drink taken the night before
optionC: Not to be under their influence to a dangerous extent
optionD: Nothing, as it is purely an employer matter
explanation: Section 13(1)(b) says an employee must not be under the influence of an intoxicant to the extent that they endanger themselves or anyone else at work.

question: Under the 2005 Act, an employer may reasonably require an employee to do what about intoxicants?
optionA: Sign a weekly sobriety declaration
optionB: Pay for their own medical check
optionC: Stay off site for a full day
optionD: Submit to an appropriate test
explanation: Section 13(1)(c) says an employee must, if reasonably required, submit to appropriate, reasonable and proportionate tests for intoxicants under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner.

question: A worker skips the safety training their employer reasonably requires. Which duty have they broken?
optionA: To attend required safety training
optionB: To prepare the site risk assessment
optionC: To notify the HSA of the project
optionD: To appoint a safety representative
explanation: Section 13(1)(f) says employees must attend the training, and undergo any assessment, that the employer reasonably requires on safety, health and welfare.

question: A worker plays a practical joke with a compressed air line. Which employee duty does this break?
optionA: To report defects as soon as possible
optionB: Not to engage in improper conduct
optionC: To attend required safety training
optionD: To cooperate with consultation
explanation: Section 13(1)(e) bans improper conduct or behaviour likely to endanger the employee or anyone else. Horseplay with air lines has caused serious internal injuries.

question: What is a safety statement?
optionA: A worker's signed account of an accident
optionB: The HSA's yearly list of the sites it will inspect
optionC: The employer's written plan for managing safety
optionD: A certificate issued at the end of Safe Pass
explanation: Section 20 requires every employer to prepare a written safety statement, based on its hazard identification and risk assessment, setting out how safety will be managed.

question: On what must an employer base its safety statement?
optionA: Last year's accident figures and nothing else
optionB: The client's design drawings for the job
optionC: The notes handed out on the Safe Pass course
optionD: Its hazard identification and risk assessment
explanation: Section 20 says the safety statement is based on the hazards identified and the risk assessment carried out under section 19 of the 2005 Act.

question: Under the 2005 Act, who may select a safety representative at a workplace?
optionA: The employees, from among themselves
optionB: The HSA inspector for the area
optionC: The client's architect on the project
optionD: The employer's insurance company
explanation: Section 25 lets employees select and appoint a safety representative from among their number to represent them in consultation with the employer.

question: On a site where more than 20 people normally work at one time, which role must the PSCS help appoint?
optionA: A first aid instructor for the site
optionB: A site safety representative
optionC: A Garda liaison officer
optionD: A county council planning inspector
explanation: Regulation 23 requires the PSCS to facilitate the appointment of a site safety representative from among the contractors' employees where more than 20 persons are normally employed at any one time.

question: Which of these may a site safety representative do?
optionA: Issue prohibition notices to the contractors
optionB: Fine contractors for unsafe practices
optionC: Investigate accidents and dangerous occurrences
optionD: Close the site by law until it is made safe again
explanation: Regulation 23 lets a site safety representative investigate accidents, dangerous occurrences and complaints and accompany inspectors. Prohibition notices are issued only by HSA inspectors.

question: A contractor normally has more than 20 people on one site. Whom must it appoint in writing?
optionA: A trade union shop steward
optionB: A second, separate PSCS
optionC: A full-time occupational nurse
optionD: A competent safety officer
explanation: Regulation 26 requires a contractor with more than 20 persons on a site, or 30 engaged in construction work, to appoint one or more competent safety officers in writing.

question: A worker raises a safety complaint and is then moved to worse shifts. Which part of the 2005 Act protects them?
optionA: The protection against penalisation
optionB: The employee's duty to report defects
optionC: The rules on the safety statement
optionD: The rule on testing for intoxicants
explanation: Section 27 says an employer must not penalise or threaten an employee for making a complaint or representation about safety, health or welfare.

question: An HSA inspector finds workers on an unguarded roof edge with a serious risk of a fall. Which notice directs that the work stop?
optionA: An improvement notice
optionB: A prohibition notice
optionC: A contravention report
optionD: A notice of intended prosecution
explanation: Under section 67 of the 2005 Act a prohibition notice is served where an activity involves or is likely to involve a risk of serious personal injury. It prohibits the activity until the matters giving rise to the risk are remedied.

question: A contractor receives an HSA improvement notice about poor welfare facilities. What must the contractor do?
optionA: Close the site at once for a week
optionB: Withdraw the workers' Safe Pass cards
optionC: Put it right within the stated time
optionD: Apply for new planning permission
explanation: Under section 66 of the 2005 Act an improvement notice states the contravention found and directs the person to remedy it by a date specified in the notice.

question: A client plans construction work lasting longer than 30 working days. What must the client do?
optionA: Inform the local Garda station
optionB: Apply for a new Safe Pass
optionC: Tell the neighbours in writing
optionD: Notify the HSA in writing
explanation: Regulation 10 requires the client to notify the HSA where work will last longer than 30 working days or exceed 500 person days.

question: Above how many person days of work must a client notify the HSA even if the job is short?
explanation: Regulation 10 sets two triggers for notification: more than 30 working days or more than 500 person days of work.

question: What does a worker normally receive on arriving at a new site, on top of Safe Pass?
optionA: A second Safe Pass course for that site
optionB: A site-specific safety induction
optionC: A full medical examination
optionD: A personal visit from the HSA
explanation: Safe Pass is general awareness. Each site's induction covers its own hazards, rules and emergency arrangements; Regulation 25 makes it a legal requirement for some workers who are exempt from Safe Pass, and sites give it to everyone in practice.

question: Does holding a Safe Pass card replace the employer's duty to train a worker for a task?
optionA: Yes, the card covers every task on site
optionB: Yes, for workers over the age of 25
optionC: No, the employer must still train them
optionD: Only for craft workers, not operatives
explanation: HSA guidance says Safe Pass is a general awareness programme and does not remove the employer's duty under the 2005 Act to give the information, instruction and training a job needs.

question: Under section 8 of the 2005 Act, the employer's general duty to keep workers safe applies how far?
optionA: Only where the HSA has already visited
optionB: Only on sites that have appointed a PSCS
optionC: Only for permanent, full-time employees
optionD: So far as is reasonably practicable
explanation: Section 8 places the general duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the safety, health and welfare at work of each of their employees.

question: A worker injured on site cannot do their normal work for more than how many days before the HSA must be told?
optionA: Three consecutive days
optionB: One working day
optionC: Seven consecutive days
optionD: Ten working days in a row
explanation: Under the 2016 reporting regulations, an injury must be reported if the employee cannot carry out normal work for more than three consecutive days, not counting the day of the accident.

question: When counting days off for an HSA accident report, how is the day of the accident treated?
optionA: It counts as a full day
optionB: It is not counted
optionC: It counts as half a day
optionD: It counts only if after noon
explanation: The HSA says the more-than-three-consecutive-days test excludes the day of the accident itself.

question: A worker is killed in a fall on site. How quickly must the HSA or the Gardaí be told?
optionA: Within 24 hours
optionB: Within five working days
optionC: Immediately
optionD: At the next safety meeting
explanation: Fatal accidents must be reported immediately to the HSA or the Gardaí, with the formal report to the HSA within five working days of the death.

question: Who has the legal duty to report a reportable injury of an employee to the HSA?
optionA: The injured worker
optionB: The worker's GP
optionC: The site's neighbours
optionD: The employer
explanation: The 2016 regulations place the duty to report on employers and the self-employed. Workers should still tell their supervisor at once so the report can be made.

question: Within what time should a non-fatal reportable accident be reported to the HSA?
optionA: Ten working days
optionB: One working day
optionC: Five working days
optionD: Thirty working days
explanation: HSA guidance says non-fatal accidents and dangerous occurrences should be reported within ten working days of the event.

question: A crane overturns on site but nobody is hurt. How is this classed for reporting?
optionA: A minor incident only
optionB: A dangerous occurrence
optionC: A near miss with no report
optionD: A design fault for the PSDP
explanation: Schedule 15 of the General Application Regulations, added by the 2016 reporting regulations, lists the collapse or overturning of lifting equipment, or failure of a load-bearing part, as a dangerous occurrence, reportable to the HSA even when nobody is injured.

question: A worker trips over a cable but is not hurt. What should they do?
optionA: Say nothing, as nobody was hurt
optionB: Report it straight to the HSA's online system
optionC: Report the near miss to the supervisor
optionD: Move the cable and forget about it
explanation: Near misses show where the next injury will come from. Reporting them lets the hazard be fixed; only reportable events go to the HSA.

question: What is the first thing to do on finding a colleague lying injured at the foot of a scaffold?
optionA: Lift them to a sitting position
optionB: Fetch them a drink of water
optionC: Take a photo for the report
optionD: Check it is safe to approach
explanation: Make sure there is no further danger, such as falling objects or live cables, before going near. Then raise the alarm and get first aid; do not move a casualty with a possible spinal injury.

question: Which phone numbers reach the emergency services in Ireland?
explanation: Both 112 and 999 connect to the emergency services in Ireland, as An Garda Síochána advises. 911 is the North American number and 000 the Australian one.

question: What information should a worker give first when calling 112 from a site?
optionA: The contractor's turnover
optionB: The site's exact location
optionC: The worker's PPS number
optionD: The time the shift began
explanation: The ambulance needs to find the site, so give the address, Eircode or directions first, then what happened and how many people are hurt.

question: Who on site should a worker go to for first aid treatment?
optionA: The nearest delivery driver on the site
optionB: The crane operator, who has a radio
optionC: The trained occupational first aider
optionD: Anyone on site who has a car
explanation: Employers must provide first aid equipment and trained occupational first aiders as the risk assessment requires. Workers should know who they are and where the kit is kept.

question: Why should the injured person's own account be written down soon after an accident?
optionA: The HSA refuses any later reports
optionB: Insurers only pay claims made that day
optionC: The card holder must sign it on the day
optionD: Memories fade and details get lost
explanation: Accurate early details help the investigation find the cause and prevent a repeat. Witness names, the time and what equipment was used should be noted.

question: After a serious accident, why should the scene be left undisturbed where safe?
optionA: So the cause can be investigated
optionB: So work can restart more quickly
optionC: So the PSDP can redesign the area
optionD: So the injured worker's card can be renewed
explanation: Apart from making things safe and helping the injured, the scene should be left as it is so the HSA and the employer can find out what went wrong.

question: What is the main purpose of investigating a site accident?
optionA: To find someone to blame
optionB: To stop it happening again
optionC: To work out who pays fines
optionD: To decide who loses their card
explanation: Investigation looks for the root causes, including unsafe systems of work, so that controls can be improved for everyone on site.

question: Where should a worker find out what to do and where to go if the fire alarm sounds on site?
optionA: From the HSA website on the day
optionB: From the client's building contract documents
optionC: In the site induction and emergency plan
optionD: From the back of the Safe Pass card
explanation: Each site has its own emergency arrangements, escape routes and assembly point, which are explained at the site-specific induction and displayed on site.

question: A site siren sounds the evacuation signal while a worker is halfway through a cut. What should they do?
optionA: Finish the cut, then leave
optionB: Collect their tools and van keys first
optionC: Wait in the canteen for further news
optionD: Make the tool safe and go to the assembly point
explanation: Stop work, make the area safe if it takes seconds, and go straight to the assembly point so the roll call can show who is missing.

question: Which extinguisher does HSA guidance list for fires involving flammable liquids such as petrol or diesel?
optionA: Foam
optionB: Water
optionC: Compressed air
optionD: A wet mop
explanation: The HSA fire extinguisher safety checks sheet lists foam for flammable liquid fires, carbon dioxide for electrical fires, and water, foam or multi-purpose powder for wood, paper and textiles. Water spreads burning liquid.

question: Smoke is coming from a site distribution board. Which extinguisher should a trained worker avoid?
optionA: Carbon dioxide
optionB: Water
optionC: Dry powder
optionD: None, as any type is fine
explanation: Water conducts electricity and can carry current back to the user. The HSA lists carbon dioxide for electrical fires; isolate the supply first if it is safe to do so.

question: A small fire starts in a waste skip. When should a trained worker try to put it out?
optionA: Always, before telling anyone else on site
optionB: Never, even if it is very small
optionC: Only if it is safe and the alarm is raised
optionD: Only once the Gardaí have arrived
explanation: Raise the alarm first. Tackle a small fire only if trained, with the right extinguisher and an escape route behind you; otherwise get out.

question: Who should be told when a worker gets a minor cut that is treated on site?
optionA: Nobody, as it is only minor
optionB: Only the HSA, within ten days
optionC: Only the worker's own GP
optionD: The supervisor, for the accident book
explanation: Every injury, however minor, should be recorded on site. Minor ones are not reportable to the HSA but the record shows patterns and protects the worker.

question: On a site, an unguarded floor opening is an example of what?
optionA: A hazard
optionB: A risk rating
optionC: A control measure
optionD: A method statement
explanation: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm, such as an open edge or a live cable. The risk is how likely and how serious the harm would be.

question: What is meant by risk?
optionA: Any object found on a building site
optionB: The likelihood and severity of harm
optionC: The money an accident would cost
optionD: The list of rules on the site board
explanation: Risk combines how likely it is that someone will be harmed by a hazard and how bad the harm could be. Controls aim to bring it down.

question: Which section of the 2005 Act requires employers to identify hazards and assess the risks?
optionA: Section 2
optionB: Section 40
optionC: Section 19
optionD: Section 77
explanation: Section 19 requires every employer to identify the hazards in the place of work, assess the risks and have a written risk assessment.

question: Under section 19 of the 2005 Act, what must the employer do after identifying the hazards?
optionA: Notify each one to the HSA
optionB: Buy PPE for every hazard
optionC: Wait for an accident to happen
optionD: Assess the risks they present
explanation: Section 19 requires the employer to identify the hazards, assess the risks and have a written risk assessment, which the safety statement is then based on.

question: In the hierarchy of control, which option comes first?
optionA: Eliminate the hazard
optionB: Issue suitable PPE
optionC: Put up a warning sign
optionD: Train the workers involved
explanation: The general principles of prevention start with avoiding the risk altogether. PPE is the last resort because it protects only the wearer and only when worn properly.

question: Why is PPE called the last line of defence?
optionA: It is the cheapest control to buy
optionB: It protects only the wearer, if used right
optionC: It removes the hazard from the site
optionD: The law bans it on most building sites today
explanation: PPE does nothing about the hazard itself. Removing or reducing the hazard, or guarding it, protects everyone and does not rely on the wearer.

question: A noisy saw is replaced with a quieter model. Which type of control is this?
optionA: Personal protection
optionB: Administrative control
optionC: Substitution
optionD: Elimination
explanation: Replacing something with a less hazardous alternative is substitution. Elimination would mean not needing the cutting at all.

question: Putting a guard rail around a stairwell opening is an example of what?
optionA: Personal protective equipment
optionB: A behaviour-based safety programme
optionC: A form of health surveillance
optionD: A collective protective measure
explanation: The general principles of prevention favour collective measures, which protect everyone, over individual measures such as harnesses.

question: A site bans deliveries during the morning start, when most workers walk in through the gate. What type of control is this?
optionA: An administrative control
optionB: An engineering control
optionC: Personal protective equipment
optionD: Elimination of the hazard
explanation: Changing how and when work is organised is an administrative control. A barrier would be an engineering control; removing vehicles altogether would be elimination.

question: When should a risk assessment be reviewed?
optionA: Only once every five years
optionB: When work or conditions change
optionC: Only after an HSA inspector visits
optionD: Never, once it has been signed
explanation: A risk assessment must be reviewed when there is a significant change, after an accident, or when there is reason to think it is no longer valid.

question: A crew is about to start a task with its own method statement. What should happen first?
optionA: They sign it without reading it
optionB: They file it until the HSA visits
optionC: They are briefed on it and follow it
optionD: They rewrite it to suit themselves
explanation: A method statement sets out the safe sequence, controls and equipment for a task. It only protects people who know what it says and follow it.

question: What is the HSA's Safe System of Work Plan (SSWP)?
optionA: A form for reporting fatal accidents to the HSA
optionB: The HSA's annual list of inspections
optionC: A pension scheme for site workers
optionD: A simple tick-box plan made before a task
explanation: The SSWP links the safety statement to the task. It uses pictograms and ticks so a crew can plan controls before each activity, even where languages differ.

question: Who should be involved in planning a task's safe system of work?
optionA: The workers who will do the task
optionB: Only the client who pays for it
optionC: Only the HSA inspector for the area
optionD: Only the architect who designed it
explanation: The people doing the job know the practical hazards. Involving them makes the plan realistic and more likely to be followed.

question: A supervisor gathers the crew for five minutes at the work face about a new hazard. What is this called?
optionA: A site induction
optionB: A toolbox talk
optionC: A safety audit
optionD: An HSA inspection
explanation: Toolbox talks are short, focused talks on one hazard or task, usually given before work or when something changes. The induction is the first briefing for a new site.

question: Most site accidents involve what kind of cause?
optionA: Faulty equipment and nothing else
optionB: Bad weather in almost every case
optionC: Unsafe acts as well as unsafe conditions
optionD: Design errors made before any work starts
explanation: Behaviour-based safety recognises that people's actions, such as rushing or taking shortcuts, play a part in most accidents alongside unsafe conditions.

question: A worker removes a guard to save time. What is this an example of?
optionA: An unsafe condition
optionB: A design control
optionC: A near miss report
optionD: An unsafe act
explanation: Removing a guard is a deliberate unsafe act. The guard being missing then becomes an unsafe condition for the next person too.

question: A worker sees a colleague about to step under a suspended load. What should they do?
optionA: Warn them straight away
optionB: Report it at the end of the day
optionC: Ignore it as it is not their trade
optionD: Take a photo for evidence
explanation: Every worker has a duty to protect others affected by their acts or omissions. Speaking up immediately prevents the injury.

question: Why are shortcuts a common cause of injury on site?
optionA: They make every job take longer
optionB: They skip the controls that protect workers
optionC: They are always reported to the HSA
optionD: They need extra paperwork afterwards for the PSCS
explanation: Shortcuts usually bypass a guard, a permit or a step in the method statement. Time pressure is a common reason people take them.

question: A job cannot be done as the method statement says. What should the worker do?
optionA: Find their own way to finish
optionB: Leave the job half done quietly
optionC: Stop and ask the supervisor
optionD: Ask another trade to do it
explanation: If the plan does not fit the conditions, stop and get it reviewed. Improvising can create risks nobody has assessed.

question: Which of these jobs would most likely need a permit to work?
optionA: Sweeping a site walkway
optionB: Stacking blocks on a pallet
optionC: Painting a site hoarding
optionD: Entering a manhole or confined space
explanation: A permit to work is a written system for high-risk tasks, setting out the precautions, isolations and checks needed before work starts and when it ends.

question: Which human factor is most likely to lead to a mistake on a long night shift?
optionA: Fatigue
optionB: Good lighting
optionC: Regular breaks
optionD: Clear instructions
explanation: Tiredness slows reactions and dulls judgement. Planning breaks and avoiding long hours reduce the risk of fatigue-related errors.

question: A new worker is unsure how to use a tool safely. What should they do?
optionA: Watch a video online and start
optionB: Ask for instruction before using it
optionC: Use it slowly and see how it goes
optionD: Borrow a more experienced worker's card
explanation: Employees must use equipment in line with their training and instructions. If they have not been shown how, they should ask before starting.

question: What does good housekeeping on site mainly prevent?
optionA: Electric shocks from cables
optionB: Noise-induced hearing loss
optionC: Slips, trips and falls
optionD: Vibration white finger
explanation: Clear walkways and tidy work areas remove the materials and waste that people trip over, one of the most common causes of site injuries.

question: Why do young and newly started workers need extra supervision?
optionA: They are not covered by the 2005 Act at all
optionB: They cannot hold a Safe Pass card
optionC: They are allowed to break site rules
optionD: They are less familiar with site hazards
explanation: Inexperienced workers have higher accident rates because they may not yet recognise hazards. Employers must assess and control the risks to them.

question: What protection must a circuit supplying portable tools at more than 125 volts have?
optionA: An RCD tripping at 30 mA or less
optionB: A fuse rated at 30 amps or more
optionC: A plug fitted with no earth pin
optionD: A longer extension lead to the board
explanation: Regulation 81 of the General Application Regulations 2007 requires residual current devices with a tripping current not over 30 milliamperes on such circuits, including those fed by generators.

question: A drill's cable is nicked and current starts flowing through the user to earth. What device should cut the supply?
optionA: A fuse in the plug top
optionB: A residual current device (RCD)
optionC: A transformer's cooling fan
optionD: An extension reel's handle
explanation: An RCD compares the current in the live and neutral conductors and disconnects quickly when some leaks away, for example through a person. A fuse protects the cable, not people.

question: Why are reduced voltage 110 V tools widely used on construction sites?
optionA: They are always battery powered
optionB: They never need any inspection
optionC: A shock from them is far less dangerous
optionD: They can be used without any plug
explanation: The General Application Regulations require a reduced low voltage supply, not over 125 V AC, for portable tools on construction sites. With the transformer midpoint earthed, a 110 V supply puts only about 55 V to earth, which the HSA says reduces the potential level of shock.

question: A worker notices a cut in the outer sheath of an extension lead. What should they do?
optionA: Wrap the cut in insulating tape
optionB: Use it only in dry weather from now on
optionC: Swap its plug onto another lead
optionD: Take it out of use and report it
explanation: Damaged leads must not be used. Report the defect so the lead is repaired or replaced by a competent person; tape is not a repair.

question: What should be checked before each use of a portable electrical tool?
optionA: Cable, plug and casing for damage
optionB: Its colour and the maker's brand
optionC: The serial number and nothing else
optionD: That it was bought in Ireland
explanation: A quick user check finds most faults: cuts or kinks in the cable, a cracked plug or casing, loose parts, and signs of burning or overheating.

question: A worker's grinder keeps cutting out. A colleague offers to open it up and fix it. What should happen?
optionA: The colleague should fix it at lunch
optionB: A competent electrician should repair it
optionC: The worker should tape the switch on
optionD: It should be used until it stops
explanation: Electrical repairs must be done by a competent person. A poor repair can leave a tool live on the casing or with no earth.

question: A long extension lead must cross a site haul road. How should it be protected?
optionA: Laid flat on the road surface
optionB: Covered with a scaffold board
optionC: Raised overhead or in a proper cable protector
optionD: Buried under loose stones
explanation: Leads crossing traffic routes must be protected from being crushed by vehicles, by running them overhead or through a purpose-made cable ramp.

question: Why is water a particular danger with electrical equipment on site?
optionA: It makes power tools much heavier
optionB: It switches off RCDs for good
optionC: It lowers the voltage of the supply
optionD: It makes electric shock more likely
explanation: Wet skin and wet surfaces lower the body's resistance, so more current flows in a shock. Keep equipment and connections dry and protected.

question: A small excavator is about to dig a trench beside a footpath. What should be done before digging starts?
optionA: Get the service drawings and scan the line
optionB: Dig a test hole by machine first
optionC: Look for warning tape after the dig
optionD: Ask the owner of the next house
explanation: HSA and ESB Networks guidance: get the service drawings, scan with a cable locator before and during the dig, and hand dig near any cable shown.

question: Near a known buried cable, how should the final digging be done?
optionA: With the excavator bucket
optionB: Carefully by hand
optionC: With a pickaxe
optionD: With a pneumatic breaker
explanation: Once a cable's position is known, expose it by careful hand digging. Mechanical excavators and picks can cut straight through cables.

question: A worker digging finds a cable that is not on the drawings. What should they do?
optionA: Cut it as it is probably dead
optionB: Move it aside by hand
optionC: Stop and treat it as live
optionD: Cover it and keep going
explanation: Treat every cable as live until a competent person proves otherwise. Stop work in that area and report it.

question: Why are overhead power lines a major hazard on sites?
optionA: They block mobile phone signals
optionB: They attract lightning and nothing else
optionC: They always carry a low voltage
optionD: Electricity can arc across a gap
explanation: High-voltage lines can arc to tipper bodies, booms, scaffold tubes and ladders that come close without touching. Many deaths involve plant under lines.

question: What should be in place where plant must pass under overhead lines?
optionA: Goal posts and barriers at a safe height
optionB: A sign telling drivers to go slowly underneath
optionC: A spotter standing on the cab roof
optionD: Nothing, if the driver is careful
explanation: The Code of Practice for Avoiding Danger from Overhead Electricity Lines requires crossing points with height-restricting goalposts of rigid, non-conducting material on each side of the line, in line with the barriers that keep plant away.

question: A tipper truck touches an overhead line. What should the driver do if it is safe to stay?
optionA: Climb down slowly holding the door
optionB: Stay in the cab until the power is off
optionC: Step out and run to get help
optionD: Touch the ground with a shovel first, then step out
explanation: The overhead lines code of practice says stop, stay in the cab, keep others away and call ESB Networks on 1800 372 999. Only if fire or another hazard forces them out should they jump clear, feet together, without touching vehicle and ground at once.

question: Who should be contacted for advice before working near ESB overhead lines?
optionA: The HSA's helpline only
optionB: The local fire brigade
optionC: ESB Networks
optionD: The Garda station
explanation: The network owner, ESB Networks, must be consulted before work near its lines. The Code of Practice for Avoiding Danger from Overhead Electricity Lines, published by ESB Networks and approved by the HSA, sets out exclusion zones and precautions.

question: Besides burns and the shock itself, what other injury does the HSA warn an electric shock can cause?
optionA: Hearing loss from the noise
optionB: Hand-arm vibration syndrome
optionC: Dermatitis from the cable
optionD: A fall, such as from a ladder
explanation: The HSA guide to the electricity regulations lists secondary injuries from muscle spasms during a shock, for example falling from a ladder after a mild shock, among the electrical hazards.

question: A labourer is stuck to a damaged live lead and cannot let go. What should a co-worker do first?
optionA: Switch off the supply
optionB: Pull them away by the arm
optionC: Throw water over them
optionD: Start CPR straight away
explanation: Touching them would put you in the circuit too. Isolate the supply, or if that is impossible move them with dry non-conductive material, then call 112 or 999, the emergency numbers the Gardaí give.

question: What should be done before work starts on an electrical installation?
optionA: Turn it down to half power
optionB: Isolate it and lock it off
optionC: Tell the client by email
optionD: Wear gloves and work live
explanation: HSA guidance on Regulation 85 says an isolator-locking device must be used so the equipment cannot become live again, and isolated conductors should be proved dead with a suitable tester at the work location before work starts.

question: Why should a worker not overload a socket with adaptors?
optionA: It lowers the voltage to the tools
optionB: It trips the scaffold's alarm
optionC: It can overheat and start a fire
optionD: It wears out the tool motor faster
explanation: Too many appliances on one outlet draw more current than it is rated for, heating the socket and cables.

question: What does an electrical warning sign on site look like?
optionA: Blue circle with a white flash
optionB: Green square with a white flash
optionC: Red circle with a black flash
optionD: Yellow triangle, black lightning flash
explanation: Warning signs are yellow triangles with black symbols. Blue circles show something you must do and red circles show something you must not do.

question: How often must an excavation be inspected while people are working in it?
optionA: At least once every day
optionB: At least once a week
optionC: At least once a month
optionD: Only when it is first dug
explanation: A competent person must inspect excavations at least once in every day during which people work there, and also after events that may affect their stability.

question: An excavation is more than 2 metres deep. When must it be inspected?
optionA: At the end of each week
optionB: At the start of each shift
optionC: Only after heavy rain
optionD: Once before the job starts
explanation: The HSA says excavations over 2 m deep must be inspected by a competent person at the start of each shift, before work begins.

question: An excavation stands unused over a holiday. How often must it still be inspected?
optionA: At least every 14 days
optionB: At least every 30 days
optionC: At least every 7 days
optionD: Not at all until it is reused
explanation: Excavations must be inspected at least once every 7 days where nobody is at work there, and again before anyone goes back in.

question: On which form does the competent person record an excavation inspection?
optionA: The Safe Pass card
optionB: The accident book
optionC: The planning notice
optionD: The AF3 form
explanation: The HSA says the competent person who inspects an excavation fills in an AF3 report on the day of the inspection.

question: Can a trench less than 1.25 m deep still need its sides supported?
optionA: Yes, if the risk assessment shows it
optionB: No, never below 1.25 m deep
optionC: Only in wet winter weather
optionD: Only if an HSA inspector asks for it
explanation: The HSA notes that poor ground or work where people lie or crouch in the trench can make support necessary even in shallow excavations.

question: What is battering an excavation?
optionA: Driving sheet piles in with a heavy hammer
optionB: Sloping the sides back to a safe angle
optionC: Filling the trench with gravel
optionD: Pumping water out of the trench
explanation: Battering cuts the sides to a slope at which the soil will not slip. Shoring or a trench box supports vertical sides instead.

question: A digger operator is about to tip spoil right at the lip of a trench where two workers are laying pipe. Why is this dangerous?
optionA: The spoil will dry out too fast
optionB: It blocks the AF3 report
optionC: The extra load can collapse the trench side
optionD: It makes the trench deeper
explanation: Spoil near the edge adds weight to the sides and can fall in. Keep spoil and materials well back from the edge.

question: A loaded tracked excavator must work beside an open trench. What should the risk assessment consider first?
optionA: Whether the operator has a radio
optionB: Whether the trench is in the shade
optionC: Whether the spoil heap is tidy
optionD: Whether the sides can bear the extra load
explanation: Heavy plant near the edge overloads the side wall and can collapse it. The machine's position, the ground and the trench support must be assessed, with barriers or stop blocks to keep it back.

question: What should surround an excavation that people could fall into?
optionA: Barriers or edge protection
optionB: Coloured tape at ankle height
optionC: Traffic cones every 20 metres
optionD: Nothing during daylight
explanation: Edge protection or barriers stop people and vehicles falling in. Tape alone does not prevent a fall.

question: A trench is too deep to step out of. What should be provided for getting in and out?
optionA: The shoring frames to climb
optionB: A ladder tied at the top
optionC: A rope hanging from the edge
optionD: The excavator bucket to ride in
explanation: The Construction Regulations require a safe means of access and egress. A ladder secured at the top and reaching above the edge, or proper steps, gives a safe route.

question: What must be inspected after a fall of earth into an excavation?
optionA: Only the heap of fallen spoil
optionB: Only the excavator that dug it
optionC: The excavation and its support
optionD: Nothing, if nobody was hurt
explanation: Any accidental fall of rock or earth, or any event likely to affect stability, triggers a fresh inspection by a competent person before work continues.

question: What can collect at the bottom of a deep excavation and make breathing dangerous?
optionA: Fresh air drawn down from the surface
optionB: Rainwater vapour and nothing else
optionC: Dust blown in from the spoil heap
optionD: Gases such as exhaust fumes
explanation: Heavier gases and fumes from engines, generators or the ground can build up in excavations. Keep engines away and test the air where needed.

question: A generator is needed for a pump in a trench. Where should it be placed?
optionA: Outside, well away from the trench
optionB: At the bottom of the trench near the pump
optionC: On the edge directly above the workers
optionD: Inside the trench box for shelter
explanation: Engine exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can build up in an excavation. Run generators outside and downwind.

question: Which nearby structure can be undermined by digging an excavation?
optionA: The radio on a tower crane
optionB: The foundations of a nearby building
optionC: The roof of the site canteen
optionD: The tyres of parked vans
explanation: Digging below or near foundations can remove their support. The risk must be assessed and the structure supported before work starts.

question: What is the main danger when water seeps into an excavation?
optionA: The trench becomes far too cold
optionB: The spoil turns into fine dust
optionC: The sides can weaken and collapse
optionD: The shoring rusts away overnight
explanation: Water softens the ground and can wash soil from behind supports. It must be pumped out safely and the sides inspected.

question: Why should nobody work ahead of the trench support as a trench is dug?
optionA: It slows the excavator down far too much
optionB: It breaks the shoring frames
optionC: It stops the spoil being moved away
optionD: Unsupported sides can collapse suddenly
explanation: A cubic metre of soil weighs over a tonne. Workers must stay within the protected area of the shoring or trench box.

question: Who should be contacted before digging near gas mains?
optionA: Gas Networks Ireland
optionB: ESB Networks only
optionC: The county library
optionD: The Road Safety Authority
explanation: Get the gas network's drawings and advice before digging. Gas mains can be damaged by excavators and cause fires or explosions.

question: What should a worker do on seeing cracks open along the edge of a trench?
optionA: Fill the cracks with loose spoil
optionB: Get everyone out and report it
optionC: Keep working but work faster
optionD: Wait to see if the cracks grow
explanation: Tension cracks are a sign the side may collapse. Get people out first, then have a competent person inspect it.

question: Which of these shows that a trench's shoring is not safe?
optionA: Struts set level and horizontal
optionB: Wedges driven tight in place
optionC: Loose wedges and bent struts
optionD: Sheets standing straight and true
explanation: HSA checks include tight wedges, horizontal struts and no excessive deflection. Loose or bent parts mean the support may fail.

question: Why should materials not be thrown into an excavation where people are working?
optionA: They spoil the AF3 inspection report
optionB: They change the type of soil
optionC: They make the trench deeper
optionD: They can strike the workers below
explanation: Materials should be lowered in a controlled way. The Construction Regulations require precautions against falling materials in excavations.

question: In Irish law, what counts as work at height?
optionA: Work anywhere a fall could cause injury
optionB: Only work more than 2 metres up
optionC: Only work done on a scaffold
optionD: Only work done on roofs, ladders and scaffolds
explanation: The HSA defines work at height as work in any place, including at or below ground level, where a person could be injured if they fell. There is no minimum height.

question: Which of these is work at height under the HSA definition?
optionA: Sitting in a site office chair
optionB: Working at ground level beside a trench
optionC: Walking up the office stairs
optionD: Driving a van along a public road
explanation: Working next to an excavation, on trestles or on a flat roof all count. Using ordinary stairs or sitting in a chair does not.

question: Which work at height measure should be chosen first?
optionA: A full body safety harness
optionB: An air bag below the work
optionC: A guard rail or working platform
optionD: A safety net under the edge
explanation: Collective measures that prevent a fall, such as guard rails and platforms, come before measures that only reduce the distance or consequences of a fall.

question: How high above the edge must the top guard rail be on construction work at height?
optionA: At least 600 mm
optionB: At least 750 mm
optionC: At least 1,500 mm
optionD: At least 950 mm
explanation: Regulation 103 of the General Application Regulations 2007 requires the top guard rail to be at least 950 mm above the edge from which a worker could fall.

question: What is the largest gap allowed between guard rails on a construction working platform?
optionA: 470 mm
optionB: 300 mm
optionC: 600 mm
optionD: 750 mm
explanation: Regulation 103 says any intermediate guard rail must be placed so that no gap between it and other protection exceeds 470 mm.

question: What do toe boards on a scaffold platform mainly prevent?
optionA: Workers slipping on the wet boards
optionB: Tools and materials falling off the edge
optionC: Rust forming on the scaffold tubes
optionD: The wind lifting the scaffold boards out of place
explanation: Toe boards stop objects being kicked or knocked off the platform onto people below, and stop a worker's foot sliding under the rail.

question: A working platform on a construction site has a fall of 2 m or more. It must have been inspected within how long before use?
optionA: The previous 14 days
optionB: The previous 28 days
optionC: The previous 7 days
optionD: The previous 3 months
explanation: Regulation 119 says such a platform must not be used unless it has been inspected in that position within the previous 7 days.

question: Apart from the regular check, when else must a scaffold be inspected?
optionA: Only when it is painted
optionB: Only when the client asks
optionC: Never after it is first built
optionD: After bad weather or damage
explanation: Work equipment for work at height must be inspected after exceptional circumstances, such as storms or impact, that could affect its safety.

question: Who may alter a scaffold on site?
optionA: A trained and competent scaffolder
optionB: Any worker who needs more room
optionC: The crane driver who lifted it in
optionD: The site electrician on duty
explanation: Removing ties, boards or rails can make a scaffold collapse or leave gaps. Scaffolding tasks are on the CSCS list and need trained scaffolders.

question: While carrying blocks along a scaffold lift, a bricklayer sees a gap where the scaffolder has removed a guard rail. What should they do?
optionA: Use the platform away from the gap
optionB: Stop and report it
optionC: Fit a spare rail themselves
optionD: Tie a rope across the gap
explanation: Do not use an incomplete scaffold or try to repair it. Report it so a competent scaffolder can complete it.

question: Under Regulation 114, when is a ladder allowed for work at height?
optionA: Any job, if the ladder is tall enough
optionB: Only jobs that involve heavy loads
optionC: Low-risk work of short duration
optionD: Only when scaffolds cost too much
explanation: A ladder may be used only where the risk assessment shows that more suitable equipment is not justified because the risk is low and the work short, or the site cannot be altered.

question: What must a ladder rest on?
optionA: Bricks stacked to gain extra height
optionB: A pallet laid on soft ground
optionC: An upturned barrel or drum
optionD: A firm, level, stable surface
explanation: Regulation 114 requires a stable, firm surface of sufficient strength so that the rungs stay level and the ladder cannot sink or slip.

question: The foot of a leaning ladder sits 0.75 m out from a wall. Roughly what height should its top rest at?
optionA: 3 metres
optionB: 1.5 metres
optionC: 2.25 metres
optionD: 4 metres
explanation: The 1 in 4 rule puts the foot one unit out for every four units up, about 75 degrees: 0.75 m out matches a rest point about 3 m up. Too shallow and the foot can slide; too steep and it can tip back.

question: A ladder is used to reach a landing. What must it do at the top?
optionA: Stop just below the landing edge
optionB: Rise far enough above it for a handhold
optionC: Rest its top on the gutter
optionD: Be tied at the bottom and at no other point
explanation: Regulation 114 requires an access ladder to protrude sufficiently above the landing unless another firm handhold is provided. The HSA guide says at least one metre beyond any landing, and the ladder secured.

question: How should a worker carry materials up a ladder?
optionA: Carry them up in both hands
optionB: Hold them under one arm while climbing
optionC: Keep a handhold and haul loads up
optionD: Throw them up to the landing first
explanation: Regulation 114 requires a secure handhold on a ladder. Heavy or bulky items should be lifted by a hoist or rope instead.

question: What should be done to stop a leaning ladder slipping?
optionA: Lean it at a shallower angle
optionB: Put a bag of sand on the top rung
optionC: Stand it on a tarpaulin
optionD: Tie it or use an anti-slip device
explanation: Regulation 114 requires portable ladders to be prevented from slipping by securing the stiles, anti-slip devices or an equivalent arrangement.

question: What should be done before using a mobile tower scaffold?
optionA: Lock the wheels
optionB: Remove the outriggers
optionC: Lean it against the wall
optionD: Let a worker ride on it
explanation: Wheels must be locked whenever the tower is in use, and nobody may stay on a mobile tower while it is moved.

question: What is a fragile surface?
optionA: A surface with fresh paint on it
optionB: A surface that could give way under you
optionC: A surface made wet by rain
optionD: A surface with a slight slope to it
explanation: Fragile roof sheets, roof lights and rotten boards can collapse under a person's weight. Falls through them cause many deaths.

question: Where is the greatest risk of falling through a roof?
optionA: Through the gutters at the eaves
optionB: Through new steel roof decking
optionC: Through roof lights and old sheeting
optionD: Through the lead flashing at a chimney
explanation: Roof lights and aged cement or plastic sheets often look solid but will not take a person's weight. They must be covered or guarded.

question: Before working near a fragile surface, what should be provided?
optionA: A harness with no anchor point
optionB: A warning sign and nothing else
optionC: A spotter standing on the ground
optionD: Platforms, covers or guard rails
explanation: Regulation 115 requires suitable platforms, coverings or guard rails where work on or near a fragile surface cannot be avoided.

question: How should a hole in a floor be protected?
optionA: With a fixed, marked cover or rail
optionB: With a loose sheet of plywood
optionC: With a traffic cone in the middle
optionD: With a sheet of plastic taped down
explanation: Covers must be strong, fixed so they cannot be moved accidentally and marked to show what they protect. A loose sheet can be lifted or slide.

question: What is the purpose of a full body harness and lanyard?
optionA: To replace guard rails on scaffolds
optionB: To arrest a fall where nothing safer works
optionC: To carry tools up a ladder safely
optionD: To keep workers warm in winter
explanation: Personal fall arrest is used only when collective measures such as guard rails and platforms are not practicable.

question: Where should a fall arrest lanyard be attached?
optionA: To a scaffold guard rail clip
optionB: To a handrail on a ladder
optionC: To a suitable anchor point
optionD: To the worker's own belt
explanation: The anchor must be strong enough to hold a falling person. The user must be connected at all times while exposed to the fall.

question: A worker on a mobile elevating platform falls and is left hanging in their harness. What must already be in place?
optionA: A second worker in a harness
optionB: A first aid kit in the van
optionC: A sign at the site gate
optionD: A rescue plan and equipment
explanation: A person hanging in a harness can suffer serious harm if left suspended. A rescue plan and equipment must be ready before work starts.

question: Waste from an upper floor must be brought down. What is the safe method?
optionA: An enclosed chute or a hoist
optionB: Throwing it over the edge
optionC: Dropping it after a shout
optionD: Rolling it down the stairs
explanation: The Construction Regulations ban throwing or dropping materials or waste from a height where they can cause injury. Use chutes, hoists or lower them in a controlled way.

question: Why is the ground below roof work fenced off with barriers and signs?
optionA: To store spare scaffold parts safely
optionB: To keep people clear of falling objects
optionC: To mark out the welfare area
optionD: To park plant overnight
explanation: Barriers and signs keep people out of the area below overhead work, where tools or materials could fall.

question: Why should work at height be stopped in high winds?
optionA: Scaffold inspections become invalid in wind
optionB: Harnesses stop working in wind
optionC: Workers and materials can be blown off
optionD: Ladders stretch in strong gusts
explanation: Strong winds can unbalance workers and lift sheets and boards. The risk assessment should set when work at height stops in bad weather.

question: Who should be the person working at height?
optionA: The youngest worker on the site
optionB: Whoever happens to be free that day
optionC: Any visitor wearing a hard hat
optionD: Someone trained and competent for it
explanation: The HSA says people working at height must be competent, and all work at height must be properly planned and organised.

question: According to the HSA, what causes the greatest number of workplace deaths in Ireland?
optionA: Accidents involving workplace vehicles
optionB: Electric shocks from hand tools
optionC: Burns from welding and hot works
optionD: Cuts from saws and hand tools
explanation: The HSA notes that accidents involving workplace vehicles cause the greatest number of workplace deaths, which is why traffic management matters on sites.

question: A 17-year-old labourer is asked to move a site dumper on his own. What does the law say?
optionA: He may if he holds a car licence
optionB: Only a competent person aged 18 or over may
optionC: He may if the foreman watches
optionD: He may on Saturdays only
explanation: The Construction Regulations 2013 say vehicles and earthmoving plant must be operated only by a competent person aged 18 or over, unless under supervised training.

question: Which card shows an operator has completed training for certain plant, such as a tower crane or excavator?
optionA: A Safe Pass card
optionB: A PPS card
optionC: A CSCS card
optionD: A first aid card
explanation: Schedule 5 of the Construction Regulations 2013 lists the CSCS tasks, including tower crane, mobile crane, telescopic handler, 180 and 360 degree excavator and dumper operation.

question: A site plans its traffic routes. Which arrangement protects people on foot best?
optionA: Shared routes with a speed sign
optionB: Workers wearing headphones
optionC: Vehicles using their horns often
optionD: Separate walkways with physical barriers
explanation: Separating people from vehicles with barriers and marked walkways is the most effective traffic control. Signs and horns only warn.

question: Why is reversing a large vehicle on site so dangerous?
optionA: The driver has large blind spots
optionB: It uses much more diesel
optionC: It wears out the tyres faster
optionD: It confuses the satellite navigation
explanation: Drivers cannot see directly behind or close beside many site vehicles. A trained signaller, cameras and one-way systems reduce reversing.

question: What does a signaller (banksman) do?
optionA: Collects the site's waste
optionB: Guides plant movements safely
optionC: Checks Safe Pass cards at the gate
optionD: Drives the delivery trucks
explanation: A signaller directs vehicle and crane movements and keeps people clear. They must wear distinctive clothing so the operator can recognise them.

question: Where should a signaller stand while guiding a reversing truck?
optionA: Directly behind the truck, close in
optionB: Inside the truck's cab, right beside the driver
optionC: In the driver's view, out of the vehicle's path
optionD: Standing on the truck's side step
explanation: The signaller must be visible to the driver at all times and in a safe position. If the driver loses sight of the signaller, the driver must stop.

question: Which standard hand signal means stop?
optionA: Both hands clasped at chest height
optionB: Left arm pointing out to the side
optionC: Both arms bent with the palms up
optionD: Right arm up, palm facing forward
explanation: Under the signals in the General Application Regulations, stop is the right arm pointing upwards with the palm forward. Hands clasped at chest height means end of operation.

question: A driver loses sight of the signaller while reversing. What must the driver do?
optionA: Stop at once
optionB: Keep going slowly
optionC: Sound the horn and continue
optionD: Speed up to finish
explanation: If the operator cannot see the signaller or cannot be sure the move is safe, they must stop and wait for new instructions.

question: May a worker ride in the bucket of an excavator to reach a high spot?
optionA: Yes, if they hold on
optionB: No, never
optionC: Yes, for short distances
optionD: Yes, if the PSCS agrees
explanation: Buckets and forks are not designed to carry people. A fall or sudden movement can kill. Use a mobile elevating work platform instead.

question: Why must dumper drivers wear a seat belt where one is fitted?
optionA: To get through a Garda checkpoint
optionB: To keep the seat clean and dry
optionC: To stay inside the roll-over protection
optionD: To stop the engine from stalling
explanation: Regulation 38 of the General Application Regulations requires roll-over protection on ride-on mobile equipment and a restraining system where the operator could be crushed if it rolls. The protection only works if the belt keeps the driver inside it.

question: What is a common cause of dumpers overturning?
optionA: Driving in a straight line on the level
optionB: Carrying no load at all
optionC: Using the handbrake when parked
optionD: Driving across or near slopes and edges
explanation: Dumpers tip on slopes, at excavation edges and on soft ground. Use stop blocks at tipping points and keep to safe routes.

question: Before leaving a vehicle on site, what should the driver do?
optionA: Lower attachments, brake on, key out
optionB: Leave the engine running
optionC: Raise the bucket fully into the air
optionD: Leave the key in for the next driver
explanation: A parked machine must be safe and secure: attachments on the ground, brake on, engine off and key removed so nobody can start it.

question: What does a flashing amber beacon on a site machine mean?
optionA: The machine is running out of fuel
optionB: The machine is working, keep clear
optionC: The driver is away on a break
optionD: The machine is for hire or for sale
explanation: Beacons warn that plant is moving or working. Stay out of its working area unless the operator knows you are there.

question: Why must people keep out of an excavator's slewing area?
optionA: The arm sprays out hydraulic oil
optionB: The tracks throw up loose stones
optionC: The rear can swing round and crush them
optionD: The cab door can swing outward suddenly on them
explanation: The counterweight swings as the machine slews and can trap a person against another object. Barriers or a signaller keep people out.

question: What must be checked on lifting equipment such as chains and slings before use?
optionA: Its colour and its length only
optionB: That it is brand new from the box
optionC: That it is the lightest one available on site
optionD: That it is marked and free from damage
explanation: The General Application Regulations require lifting accessories to be marked so the characteristics essential for safe use can be identified, and to be thoroughly examined at set intervals. Damaged ones are taken out of use.

question: A crane is lifting steel beams over the area where a crew wants to keep working. What should happen?
optionA: The crew moves clear until the lift is done
optionB: They keep working with hard hats on
optionC: They work under it if the load is small
optionD: They hold the beam by hand to guide it
explanation: A hard hat will not protect against a falling load. Keep clear of suspended loads and use tag lines to steady them from a safe position.

question: What is the safe working load (SWL) of lifting equipment?
optionA: The weight of the equipment itself
optionB: The most it may lift safely
optionC: The load it can lift in an hour
optionD: The lightest load it can handle
explanation: Regulation 48 requires machinery for lifting loads to be clearly marked with its safe working load and not used beyond it except when tested under a competent person.

question: A guard is missing from a bench saw. What should a worker do?
optionA: Use it with extra care
optionB: Wear gloves and carry on
optionC: Not use it and report it
optionD: Ask a colleague to hold the timber
explanation: Machinery guards prevent contact with moving parts. The saw must not be used until the guard is refitted by a competent person.

question: What should be worn when using an angle grinder?
optionA: Loose gloves and no safety glasses
optionB: A tie to keep the shirt tidy
optionC: Shorts and a T-shirt for comfort
optionD: Eye protection, with the guard fitted
explanation: Disc fragments and sparks cause serious eye injuries. Keep the guard on, use the correct disc and wear eye protection; loose clothing can catch.

question: How often must lifting accessories such as chains, hooks and shackles be thoroughly examined?
optionA: At least every 6 months
optionB: At least every 5 years
optionC: Only when they are new
optionD: Only after an accident
explanation: Schedule 1 of the General Application Regulations 2007 sets a thorough examination by a competent person at least every 6 months for lifting accessories such as chains, ropes, hooks and shackles.

question: A crane must be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least how often?
optionA: Every 5 years
optionB: Every 12 months
optionC: Every 10 years
optionD: Only when first bought
explanation: Schedule 1 of the General Application Regulations 2007 sets a thorough examination of a crane at least every 12 months, alongside its regular checks.

question: A hoist is repaired in a way that affects its safe operation. What must happen before it is used again?
optionA: A labourer test-lifts a full load
optionB: The repairer signs the site diary only
optionC: A competent person must examine it
optionD: Nothing, if the hoist runs smoothly
explanation: Regulation 52 of the General Application Regulations requires lifting equipment to be examined by a competent person before returning to service after a repair or alteration relevant to its safe operation.

question: How should a delivery truck driver be managed on arrival at a site?
optionA: Left to find their own way around
optionB: Told to reverse into the nearest gap
optionC: Allowed to park on the footpath
optionD: Met and directed under the traffic plan
explanation: Site traffic management plans set the routes, unloading areas and signaller arrangements for deliveries so drivers and workers are kept safe.

question: A worker's daily noise exposure reaches 82 dB(A). What must the employer do as a minimum?
optionA: Make hearing protection available
optionB: Nothing until 90 dB(A)
optionC: Stop the work immediately
optionD: Move the worker to nights
explanation: 80 dB(A) is the lower exposure action value in the General Application Regulations 2007, at which hearing protection must be made available. At 85 dB(A) it must be worn.

question: Above which daily noise exposure must hearing protection zones be marked and protection worn?
optionA: 75 dB(A)
optionB: 85 dB(A)
optionC: 80 dB(A)
optionD: 90 dB(A)
explanation: At the upper exposure action value of 85 dB(A) the employer must make sure hearing protection is used, and the areas are marked as hearing protection zones.

question: What daily noise exposure must never be exceeded at the ear, even allowing for hearing protection?
optionA: 80 dB(A)
optionB: 85 dB(A)
optionC: 87 dB(A)
explanation: 87 dB(A) is the exposure limit value in the Irish noise regulations, assessed taking account of the hearing protection worn.

question: What rough test suggests noise in an area is above the action level?
optionA: A radio can be heard from indoors
optionB: A phone ringing goes unnoticed once
optionC: The noise lasts for over an hour
optionD: Shouting is needed to talk at 2 metres
explanation: The HSA says if it is difficult to hear normal conversation at 2 metres, the noise is likely to be above 80 dB(A).

question: What is the main long-term effect of repeated loud noise at work?
optionA: Permanent hearing loss
optionB: Short-sightedness
optionC: Dermatitis on the hands
optionD: Weakened bones in old age
explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss builds up over years and cannot be cured. Tinnitus, a ringing in the ears, is another lasting effect.

question: Which of these tools is most likely to cause hand-arm vibration syndrome?
optionA: A spirit level or square
optionB: A breaker or an angle grinder
optionC: A tape measure or chalk line
optionD: A paint brush or roller
explanation: Hand-held powered tools such as breakers, grinders and hammer drills pass vibration into the hands and arms.

question: What is vibration white finger?
optionA: A skin rash caused by wet cement
optionB: Frostbite from working in very cold weather
optionC: Finger circulation damaged by vibration
optionD: A fungal infection of the nails
explanation: Vibration white finger is part of hand-arm vibration syndrome. Fingers go white and numb, especially in the cold, and the damage can be permanent.

question: Which early sign of hand-arm vibration syndrome should a worker report?
optionA: Sore feet at the end of a shift
optionB: A stiff neck first thing in the morning
optionC: Sunburn on the backs of the arms
optionD: Tingling or numbness in the fingers
explanation: The HSA says workers should be trained to recognise and report numbness and tingling early, before the condition worsens.

question: What is the daily exposure action value for hand-arm vibration?
optionD: 5 m/s² A(8)
explanation: The General Application Regulations 2007 set the hand-arm action value at 2.5 m/s² and the limit at 5 m/s². 0.5 and 1.15 are the whole-body values.

question: Which step reduces hand-arm vibration exposure most?
optionA: Wearing anti-vibration gloves
optionB: A different method or a low-vibration tool
optionC: Gripping the tool much harder
optionD: Working faster to finish sooner
explanation: The HSA says to avoid the process or use lower-vibration tools and less trigger time. It does not count anti-vibration gloves as a control, though gloves keep hands warm.

question: Why does keeping hands warm help a worker who uses vibrating tools?
optionA: It lowers the tool's own vibration
optionB: It makes the tool feel lighter
optionC: It keeps blood flowing to the fingers
optionD: It stops dust reaching the skin
explanation: Cold narrows the blood vessels and makes vibration damage worse. Warm gloves and warm breaks help circulation.

question: Which illness can workers catch from rat urine on sites and in water?
optionA: Legionnaires' disease
optionB: Tetanus from rusty nails
optionC: Hepatitis A from food
optionD: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease)
explanation: Leptospirosis enters through cuts or the eyes and mouth. Cover cuts, wash hands before eating and keep welfare areas clean.

question: What should a worker do on finding material they suspect is asbestos?
optionA: Stop work and report it
optionB: Break a piece off to check it
optionC: Sweep it up and bin it
optionD: Wet it and keep cutting
explanation: The HSA says that if you uncover hidden material or dust you suspect may contain asbestos, stop work and get competent advice. Disturbing it releases fibres that can cause cancer.

question: How should silica dust from cutting concrete be controlled?
optionA: Cutting faster to finish sooner
optionB: Water suppression or on-tool extraction
optionC: Opening the site gates for air
optionD: Brushing the dust away afterwards
explanation: Respirable crystalline silica causes lung disease. Wet cutting or on-tool extraction stops dust at source; RPE is added where needed.

question: Why should workers outdoors protect their skin from the sun?
optionA: Sunlight makes their PPE fade
optionB: Sunlight weakens the scaffold tubes
optionC: Skin cancer is common in outdoor workers
optionD: Sunlight drains tool batteries
explanation: The HSA says skin cancer is the most common cancer in Ireland and more common in outdoor workers. Cover up, use sunscreen and take shade.

question: What is the most common cause of manual handling injuries?
optionA: Lifting with the knees bent
optionB: Keeping the load close to the body as you lift
optionC: Planning the route before lifting
optionD: Lifting with a bent back or twisting
explanation: Bending and twisting while lifting strains the back. Keep the load close, bend the knees, avoid twisting and get help or a lifting aid.

question: What should an employer do first about heavy manual handling?
optionA: Avoid it with mechanical aids
optionB: Train everyone to lift more weight
optionC: Hand out back support belts
optionD: Rotate the strongest workers
explanation: The General Application Regulations require employers to avoid manual handling where possible, for example with hoists, trolleys and smaller loads.

question: Which welfare facility must a construction site provide?
optionA: A gym for the workforce
optionB: Toilets and washing facilities
optionC: Free car parking for all
optionD: A covered smoking shelter
explanation: The Construction Regulations 2013 require sanitary conveniences, washing facilities with hot and cold or warm running water, potable drinking water, a sheltered place to take meals and a way of drying wet clothing.

question: A plasterer goes straight from mixing to eating a sandwich in the van. What is the health risk?
optionA: Catching a cold from the van
optionB: Damaging their hearing
optionC: Swallowing harmful substances
optionD: Straining their back
explanation: Cement, lead, oils and bacteria on the hands can be swallowed with food. Washing hands before eating removes them.

question: What skin problem can wet cement cause?
optionA: Vibration white finger
optionB: Noise-induced hearing loss
optionC: Sunstroke and heat stress
optionD: Dermatitis and burns
explanation: Wet cement is alkaline and can cause dermatitis and chemical burns. Wear gloves and long sleeves and wash off any cement promptly.

question: Who must normally pay for PPE that a worker needs on site?
optionA: The employer
optionB: The worker
optionC: The HSA
optionD: The client's insurer
explanation: Section 8(5) of the 2005 Act says safety measures must not involve financial cost to employees, and Regulation 62 of the General Application Regulations requires employers to provide PPE where risks cannot be avoided by other means.

question: What is a worker's duty when PPE is provided?
optionA: Wear it only when inspectors visit
optionB: Wear and use it properly, as trained
optionC: Lend it to visitors who need it
optionD: Alter it to make it more comfortable
explanation: Section 13 of the 2005 Act requires employees to make correct use of PPE provided for their protection, in line with training and instructions.

question: Which colour and shape of sign tells a worker that a hard hat must be worn?
optionA: Red circle with a bar
optionB: Yellow triangle
optionC: Blue circle
optionD: Green rectangle
explanation: Blue circles are mandatory signs showing something you must do. Red circles with a bar prohibit, yellow triangles warn and green signs show safe conditions.

question: A hard hat issued to one worker is to be given to another. What must happen first?
optionA: It must be painted a new colour
optionB: It must be signed by the HSA
optionC: Nothing, any hat can be shared
optionD: It must be cleaned and disinfected
explanation: Regulation 35 of the Construction Regulations 2013 says a helmet must not be issued to any other person until it has been cleaned and disinfected.

question: What must every hard hat issued on a construction site be marked with?
optionA: A mark identifying who it was issued to
optionB: The site's planning number
optionC: The client's company logo
optionD: The date of the next HSA visit
explanation: Regulation 35 of the Construction Regulations 2013 requires each protective helmet to carry a distinguishing mark identifying it with the person it was issued to.

question: What do safety boots with a midsole protect against?
optionA: Electric shocks from cables
optionB: Nails piercing the sole
optionC: Noise from breakers
optionD: Cold weather only
explanation: A penetration-resistant midsole stops nails and sharp objects coming up through the sole; the toecap protects against falling objects.

question: Why do dumper and excavator operators need workers on foot to wear high-visibility clothing?
optionA: So their trade can be identified
optionB: So they stay warm in winter
optionC: So they can be seen against the site
optionD: So their Safe Pass can be checked
explanation: High-visibility clothing makes people stand out against the site background, especially near moving vehicles and in poor light.

question: What should a worker check before wearing ear defenders?
optionA: That they match the hard hat's colour
optionB: That they are the loudest type available
optionC: That music can play through them
optionD: That the seals are intact and clean
explanation: Cracked or dirty seals let noise through. Ear defenders must fit properly and be worn all the time in noisy areas to work.

question: Why must earplugs be inserted properly?
optionA: A poor fit lets noise through
optionB: They can fall deep into the ear
optionC: They block the air flow to the brain
optionD: They can damage the eardrum
explanation: Earplugs only work when correctly fitted. Roll, insert and hold as trained, with clean hands.

question: What must be done before a tight-fitting dust mask is relied on?
optionA: A blood test
optionB: A face fit test
optionC: An eye test
optionD: A hearing test
explanation: HSA guidance recommends fit testing for all tight-fitting respirators, to make sure the mask seals to the individual wearer. A tight seal at all times is vital to prevent exposure.

question: A worker with a beard needs respiratory protection. What does HSA guidance say?
optionA: Use a tight-fitting mask pulled tighter
optionB: Use two disposable masks at once
optionC: Use a type with no face seal, such as a hood
optionD: Go without, as no mask will work
explanation: HSA guidance says tight-fitting respirators must not be worn by people with a beard or moustache, because air leaks past the seal. Respirators that do not rely on a tight seal, such as hoods or helmets, may be used instead.

question: Which eye protection is needed when using a disc cutter?
optionA: Ordinary tinted sunglasses
optionB: The worker's reading glasses
optionC: None if working outdoors
optionD: Impact-rated glasses or goggles
explanation: Flying fragments need impact-rated eye protection. Ordinary glasses can shatter and do not protect the sides of the eyes.

question: What should a worker do if their PPE is damaged?
optionA: Report it and get it replaced
optionB: Repair it with tape and carry on
optionC: Keep using it until the job ends
optionD: Throw it away and work without it
explanation: Damaged PPE may not protect. Employees must report defects, and employers must maintain and replace PPE.

question: Which gloves suit handling wet concrete?
optionA: Thin cotton work gloves
optionB: Waterproof gloves rated for cement
optionC: Leather welding gauntlets
optionD: Fingerless wool gloves for keeping warm
explanation: Cotton soaks up wet cement and holds it against the skin. Waterproof, cement-resistant gloves with long cuffs protect against burns.

question: Why must PPE be compatible when several items are worn together?
optionA: It must all be the same colour
optionB: It must all come from one brand
optionC: One item can stop another working
optionD: It must all weigh about the same
explanation: For example, safety glasses can break the seal of ear defenders, or a hard hat may not fit with a visor. PPE must be chosen to work together.

question: How should PPE be stored when not in use?
optionA: In the back of a hot van
optionB: On the ground beside the mixer
optionC: Under heavy materials in the yard
optionD: Clean, dry and away from damage
explanation: Heat, sunlight, chemicals and crushing degrade PPE. Proper storage keeps it fit for use.
